newsitem.title: GERMANY: Signs of end to German property slump - survey.
newsitem.headline: Signs of end to German property slump - survey.

text.p: Tentative signs that the post-unification slump in Germany's commercial property market may be coming to an end emerged in a survey of market expectations published on Monday.

Frankfurt-based property consultancy DTZ Zadelhoff said its spring 1997 survey of banks, property investors and developers showed "increasing stability and the first positive signs" of a market recovery, if only in the west of the country.
In the recession-hit east, where state subsidies have financed large increases in new property building, heavy over-capacity will continue to depress rents, it added.

The survey of over 100 respondents showed that while the majority still said the overall market mood was "negative", fewer participants were still pessimistic about the crucial office property market compared to last autumn.

DTZ Deutschland chairman Michael Koch said foreign investors, who deserted in droves when it emerged that German unification in 1990 would not be a major spur to the economy, now even rated the office sector as "satisfactory".
"Foreign investors were the first to recognise the slump in office property around 1991. Perhaps they are also the first to sense a market movement upwards today," Koch told a news briefing.
Koch said international investors, particularly Dutch, British and Swedish, had over the last few years pulled out of German property to reinvest in higher-yielding markets.
German office property yields have been stuck at a relatively unattractive five to six percent as rents have in some cases virtually halved over the last four years.

In Berlin, which as capital of the enlarged country was thought to have most to gain from unification, office property that in 1993 cost close to 70 marks a square metre was now available at just over 40 marks, DTZ said.

And in eastern cities such as Leipzig or Dresden, prime office accommodation now cost as little as 25 marks a square metre compared to well over 50 marks in Frankfurt, the country's most expensive town to set up office.

Highlighting the continued economic gap between east and west Germany, DTZ said nobody in its survey expected rent increases in the east of the country this year, while a substantial proportion thought Frankfurt, Munich and, to a lesser extent Hamburg, could see rental growth.
